title: Course Syllabus
text:
Catalog description
This course provides a treatment of advanced topics in Data Science. Topics include: (i) Privacy and Ethics, (ii) Multivariate Statistics, (iii) Big Data and Cloud Computing, and (iv) Deep Learning. The course will draw from numerous case studies and applications, with a practical rather than theoretical emphasis.

Typical project deliverables include shared code of ethics with reflection, a presentation (Project 3 / final slot), and a written report with code appendix—exact prompts will be posted under projects.

title: Course Syllabus
text:
Academic integrity
Students are responsible for knowing and abiding by Cal Poly Humboldt’s academic honesty policy. Students caught cheating will receive zero points and be reported to Student Judicial Affairs. Working in small groups on projects and when preparing for quizzes is encouraged, but work submitted for grading must be your own.

title: Course Syllabus
text:
AI policy
You may use AI (for example ChatGPT or Claude) to help you learn the materials, perform data analyses, or work on projects. For graded work completed outside class:

If you used AI, acknowledge it briefly in the document (name the service; detailed prompts are not required).
You are responsible for the correctness and appropriateness of everything you turn in (AI-assisted or not).

The instructor may use AI to improve course materials (for example checking whether an assignment is college-level or clarifying quiz wording). AI will not be used to grade your work, and AI detection tools will not be used to check your work.

title: Course Syllabus

Learning outcomes

Program / student learning outcomes (summary)
Students will demonstrate computational skills to extract and visualize data; statistical knowledge to build models and ensure valid analysis; contemporary data-oriented skills with ethical considerations; and effective communication for diverse audiences.


Course learning outcomes
Upon successfully completing this course, you will be able to apply advanced data science methods and ethical reasoning in practical case studies spanning privacy, multivariate statistics, big data / cloud computing, and deep learning.

title: Quiz 1 study bank
text:
Download this page as PDF
The Friday quiz will have a few of these questions. Work the set. This first quiz will be graded on participation, not correctness.
Reading: Hundred-Page Language Models Book Ch. 1.
Lab: Lab 1 notebook.

From the Reading:

[Concept] Consider the general model \(y=f(x)\). What are \(x\), \(y\), and \(f\) in supervised learning? (§1.2)
[Concept] List the four steps of the supervised ML process. (§1.3)
[Concept] Why do we need a loss function? Give one example of a loss function that is appropriate for linear regression. (§1.2–§1.3)
[Math] Rewrite \(y = wx + b\) for two features using vector notation. (§1.4)
[Math] For \([1,0]\) and \([0,1]\): compute cosine similarity and say whether the vectors point the same way. (§1.4)
[Concept] Are “parameters” and “weights” used interchangeably in this chapter? What are the parameters in \(y=wx+b\)? (§1.2)
[Concept] In logistic regression, consider the standard meaning of \(z\), \(\hat p\), \(\hat y\), and \(y\). Which is the logit, the predicted probability, the predicted label, and the observed label? (§1.7–§1.8 + Lab 1)
[Math] Write the logistic model in standard notation and the sigmoid \(\sigma(z)\). (§1.7)
[Math] Write the equation for binary cross-entropy for one example. (§1.7)
[Concept] Why do we have to use iterative optimization (like gradient descent) for logistic regression? (§1.7)



Lab / code

[Code] What does loss.backward() compute, and what does optimizer.step() do next?
[Code] In
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(2, 1),
    nn.Sigmoid()
)
what do 2 and 1 represent? Which tensor is \(z\), and which is \(\hat p\)? How do you get \(\hat y\) from \(\hat p\)?
[Math] Suppose we have layer = nn.Linear(12, 1). How many trainable numbers (weights + bias) are in this layer? If the input has shape (32, 12), what is the output shape?
[Lab] Suppose that network has almost zero training loss on a tiny dataset. Name a potential problem.

title: Project 1
text:
Download this page as PDF
Due (full package): Friday, October 2
Weight: 20% of the course (stepping stones count toward this project, not toward labs)
Wildfire insurance AI lab: a risk model (Model 1) and later an evidence-to-text model (Model 2). Weeks 1–2 are only Model 1.

Target (do not loosen this language)
We estimate
\[\mathbb{P}(\texttt{serious\_damage}=1 \mid \text{structure inspected in or near a wildfire perimeter})\]
using de-identified CAL FIRE DINS construction features (and later, optional location-derived hazard layers).
serious_damage is 1 for Major or Destroyed, 0 for No Damage / Affected / Minor. Inaccessible rows are out of the supervised table.
This is not an annual household loss probability, not a premium, and not a coverage decision. A separate rule (threshold / abstain / specialist review) will turn scores into an action. Model 2 may describe that action; it may not invent coverage.


Stepping stones



Stone
Due
What you turn in




Week 1
Wed Sep 2, 11:59 p.m.
Contract + PyTorch logistic baseline





Model 1 in PyTorch
Same loop as The Hundred-Page Language Models Book and Karpathy:
optimizer.zero_grad()
logits = model(x)                 # z, not probabilities
loss = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()(logits, y)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

Week 1: nn.Linear(n_features, 1) — logistic, \(z = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b\).
Week 2: a small MLP (RiskMLP) with the same loss.

Do not use sklearn for the graded Model 1 fits. Encoding categoricals with pandas is fine.


Data
You will receive a de-identified table (properties_modeling.csv) with a split column (train / validation / test). Fit on train, make choices on validation, leave test until the final package.
The instructor table is built from public CAL FIRE DINS. Street, APN, and coordinates are stripped before you see it.


Labs vs this project
Tuesday labs are ungraded Colab notebooks (practice for the Friday paper quiz). They are not stepping stones. The stones on this page are the project checkpoints.

title: Project 1 — Week 1 stepping stone
text:
3. PyTorch logistic baseline
Fit logistic regression in PyTorch. Lab 1 used the book’s Sequential + Sigmoid + BCELoss on a toy example. This stone uses the numerically stabler wrapper: one linear layer, logits, BCEWithLogitsLoss (same \(\hat y = \sigma(z)\)).
Use the instructor table and the supplied split column. Fit on train. Report on validation (leave test alone).
import torch
from torch import nn

model = nn.Linear(n_features, 1)          # z = Wx + b
criterion = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-3)

optimizer.zero_grad()
logits = model(x).squeeze(-1)             # (B,)
loss = criterion(logits, y)               # y in {0, 1}
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
Do not use sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression for this stone. DATA 322 already did the closed-form / sklearn version; here the point is the training loop you will reuse for the MLP.
Report:

training-set prevalence of serious_damage;
validation loss, and either ROC-AUC or Brier score;
a confusion table at one probability threshold you chose;
one sentence on why that threshold is a decision, not a property of \(z\).

title: Project 1 — Week 1 stepping stone
text:
4. One training-loop check
Paste a few lines showing zero_grad → forward → loss.backward() → optimizer.step(), and state which of those produces \(\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}\mathcal{L}\).
